idiom_name: jakarta.servlet.Filter + FilterChain, ordered by the container (Spring Security SecurityFilterChain)
implementation_notes: The platform supplies the chain: the servlet container builds a FilterChain per request and each Filter's doFilter inspects or wraps the request, short-circuits by not calling chain.doFilter, or passes control inward; Spring Security layers its own ordered SecurityFilterChain over the same mechanism with authentication filters ahead of the authorisation filter. What replaces the classic structure: the container's FilterChain replaces the hand-written proxy chain and Spring's DSL replaces the wiring code - register one filter per boundary or concern and let the container compose them; hand-written proxy classes remain justified when the protected object is an in-process service interface rather than an HTTP request, which is the dynamic-proxy variant.
pitfalls: A filter declared as a bean is registered with the embedded container as well as with the security chain, so it can run twice or in an order nobody intended; disable the container registration explicitly.
Filters that wrap the request to expose the verified principal publish it as a request attribute that any downstream code can overwrite.
Ordering is the policy: an authorisation filter placed before the authentication filter sees no principal, and a permissive fallback there silently fails open.

variants.name: JDK dynamic proxy with an InvocationHandler per gate
variants.implementation_notes: When the protected thing is an in-process service interface rather than an HTTP request, the JDK generates the proxy: Proxy.newProxyInstance returns an object implementing the interface whose every call is dispatched to an InvocationHandler, so a gate is a handler that checks the invoked Method and arguments (and any annotation on them) and then invokes the next handler or the target through reflection. What replaces the classic structure: reflection removes the hand-written forwarding methods entirely, and gates nest by wrapping handlers; the verbosity and the checked-exception rules of reflection are the price, and the servlet filter chain remains the default in web applications.
pitfalls: Reflection wraps the target's exceptions in InvocationTargetException; a gate that forwards that wrapper changes the interface's error contract and hides denials from callers.
Only interface methods are intercepted - calls made internally by the target, final classes and self-invocation never pass the handler.
Duplicated method signatures across interfaces resolve to the first interface's Method object, so annotation-based rules must not assume which interface the caller used.
